thread.title: General Motors: Excellent Execution, Underestimated Upside And Overly Conservative Valuation - General Motors Company (NYSE:GM)

author: Vladimir Dimitrov, CFA
title: General Motors: Excellent Execution, Underestimated Upside And Overly Conservative Valuation - General Motors Company (NYSE:GM)
text:
Source: Autonews
Investment Thesis Investing in industries shaken up by disruption is considered quite risky; however, opportunities in such disrupted sectors often exist as it is exactly in these sectors where investors tend to get very emotional and often get carried away by promised castles in the air. Disruption often causes markets to act irrational giving some companies lofty valuations based on promises while beating down others on the grounds that they would simply stand still and get disrupted. Well, that is exactly why I chose to invest in a company labelled a "dinosaur" of its time and decided to pass on other red hot competitors.
General Motors (NYSE: GM ), often perceived as a slow moving, old-fashioned, traditional ICE car & truck manufacturer, is transforming itself significantly faster than what the market is pricing at the moment. Only two years after the acquisition of the Silicon Valley start-up Cruise Automation in May 2016 for a total amount of $581m, the GM division is now valued at $11.5bn or $10.1bn after taking into account the time value of money.
GM's high margin in Crossovers and Trucks is benefiting heavily from the prolonged cycle and the shift in customers' purchasing behavior. The high cash generation has allowed GM to restructure its international operations and position itself for the industry transition period while also sustaining its cash balance and funding its future endeavors in Autonomous and Electric Vehicles.
The leaner structure of GM with focus on two of the largest markets – U.S. and China - coupled with its strong position in the high margin SUV business, Electric and Autonomous Vehicles creates a unique competitive advantage. The in-house development of the self-driving AI also gives GM a huge leverage in future partner negotiations and contrasts with other auto manufacturers that merely provide “dumb cars” to those having the AI in place.
All that comes at a conservative valuation which to a large extent already prices in future slow-down in sales.
Disruption for some, opportunity for others As giants such as Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and SoftBank ( OTCPK:SFTBY ) are all lucratively looking at the sector, one thing is becoming clear – you can’t go alone in this huge endeavor of providing large scale autonomous mobility. That’s why we have seen a flurry of deals and partnerships in the AV and ridesharing space: BMW with Intel and Fiat , Daimler & Bosch , SoftBank & GM , Waymo & Jaguar , Toyota & Uber , Ford & Lyft etc.
It’s perhaps not surprising that all of those listed above, except Toyota, are now leading the market:
Source: Navigant Research
Quite surprisingly, GM, the company labelled "slow moving dinosaur," appears at the top right-hand corner with the likes of Waymo and Daimler-Bosch. But that alone is not a reason to pull the trigger and go for GM or Waymo.
Firstly, the whole market for AVs has a huge potential and there would be a place for a large number of players. Goldman Sachs estimates the market size of self-driving cars to amount to $96bn by 2025 and it seems unlikely that 1 or 2 players would be able to capture this entire stake for themselves. Especially when considering the huge competition from deep pocket tech behemoths such as Apple, Google and SoftBank.
Secondly, the AV market is not likely to be a profitable business for quite a while. It would require an enormous amount of future investments, while benefits, as high as they might be, would take time.
So why GM then?
1. Contrary to popular belief, GM creates significant value In May 2016, GM acquired Cruise Automation for $581m - $291m in cash and $290m in GM stock. Undoubtedly, GM has dedicated additional funds to Cruise Automation afterwards – to supply it with its latest Chevy Bolt vehicles, to acquire the lidar company Strobe , etc. However, following up from the SoftBank investment this whole investment is now valued at around $11.5bn , based on the $2.25bn investment for a 19% stake.
The $11.5bn is an overstatement in my opinion, as of the whole investment of $2.25bn, only $900m will be received now and the other $1.35bn when Cruise Automation AVs are ready for commercial deployment. Assuming a 12% discount rate (the same Damodaran uses for valuing Uber ( UBER )) and a two-year period for commercial deployment (although GM expects that to be 2019), I come up with a value of $10.1bn. So even after accounting for the additional $1.1bn that GM has committed to invest and the funds provided by SoftBank, that’s more than 300% annual growth rate on the original investment.
2. A deal that differs and brings an important partner From all the key partnership agreements listed above, the one between GM and SoftBank stands out – it’s actually an investment. It’s the tech giant SoftBank that invests in GM’s division as opposed to a partnership aiming at catching up with the current leader Waymo. It also contrasts with the Waymo Jaguar Land Rover deal in which Jaguar will provide the cars while the driver (the AI capability) will remain with Google.
Of course, SoftBank will probably not constrain itself only to providing the funds, but would rather try to integrate GM CruiSe more heavily with some of its other investments:
Source : Where SoftBank has invested its $100 billion Vision Fund
3. Business Structure & Management A key competitive advantage of GM has been its high margin SUV and Truck business. The shift in customers’ purchasing behavior from small cars to Crossovers has given GM and other companies such as Ford (NYSE: F ) and Fiat Chrysler (NYSE: FCAU ) the much-needed cash to prepare for the upcoming industry transition. GM didn't only do a great job in improving its self-driving car technology, but it also excelled in the Pickup Truck & Crossover markets with the new Silverado which is the second best-selling pickup for Q1 2018 and the Chevrolet Equinox . In its efforts to fully capitalize on the ongoing trend, GM has also improved the fuel efficiency of its Silverado and GMC Sierra pickups by offering these models with four-cylinder engines .
Moreover, GM has also re-positioned itself geographically by focusing on its main market – the U.S. while also pushing aggressively in China through its JV network with SAIC and Wuling. The sale of its Opel Vauxhall division , closing down the Holden plant and the deal of its South Korean units were all painful developments in the eyes of many investors; however, all these restructuring efforts have now made GM better prepared to focus on the future.
It’s the management that has done all that over the course of only two years, while also keeping GM’s Chevy Bolt on the heels of Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ).
Last but not least, GM's team is rapidly evolving, attracting talent from the mecca of the U.S. high tech industry - Silicon Valley.
Source: Fortune
The downside Before I go into the valuation, I would like to first cover the major risks facing GM – peaking car sales in the U.S. and the large lease exposure.
Car Sales Cycle in the U.S.
The peak in car sales in the U.S. is one of the main reasons why GM and most of its competitors now trade at such a ridiculously low multiples.
Source: FRED
Source: Yahoo
As many analysts, commentators and fellow Seeking Alpha authors are righteously suggesting, auto sales in the U.S. are peaking and might even be reaching an all-time high. It is a real possibility, although trying to time large macro trends has always been a foolish game, especially in an industry that is facing so much transformation at the moment.
Just looking at the graph above the two major downturns in US car sales – in 2008 and 1990 coincided with the two recessions in the country, while the recession of 2001 did not have any material impact. Moreover, as the last cycle peaked around 1999 it took almost 10 years until we saw a meaningful decline.
To get some idea of how vehicle sales numbers relate to valuation metrics I looked at Ford’s historical P/E ratio. The reason why I looked at Ford is that old GM faced bankruptcy during the last recession and Fiat Chrysler data is not comparable over this whole period as it used to be part of DaimlerChrysler.
Source: FRED & Ycharts
The red line is median P/E ratio over periods when it experienced significant increase/decrease. Of course, we have to bear in mind that there are many factors affecting the P/E ratio, such as idiosyncratic risks, interest rates, EPS forecasts, etc. However, there are a few observations that could be made:
Before the end of the last cycle we saw much more elevated median P/E ratio than Ford's current one, despite the higher interest rates at that time and lower S&P 500 P/E multiple. There is further downside risk of the P/E ratio, should we witness a meaningful decline in total auto sales caused by a recession. Let’s face it, a recession in the U.S. is a real possibility as the yield curve is flattening but if we see a major downturn in economic activity the whole auto manufacturing sector would decline and no company would be spared, especially the likes that are massively unprofitable and burn huge amounts of cash.
Another argument for the peak in auto sales is that as AVs and ridesharing trends accelerate, we are likely to see a meaningful decrease in vehicle sales. Again, another long-term speculation that seems to oversimplify the whole trend. We are too early in this long-term development and as Michael Ronen from Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS ) points out , the usage of cars is likely to change dramatically, so it’s too early to tell whether the whole number of sales would go up or down.
Another point to consider here is that even if the total vehicle sales decline as a result of that trend, margins are likely to be much higher as cars turn into moving supercomputers packed with lots of IP which would naturally increase margins of those owning it, in GM’s case – GM Cruise.
In a nutshell, I try to avoid timing long-term trends and stay focused on companies having a real competitive advantage at a discounted price. My answer to the fears of recession, on the other hand, is simple - portfolio diversification.
Leases & Inventory levels Another major risk for GM is the company’s significant lease exposure.
Source: GM 10k filings
Equipment on operating leases has expanded dramatically over the past few years reaching 20% of Total Assets. This compares to merely 12% in the case of Ford:
Source: Ford Annual Report 2017
Although number of leases for all three types of vehicles – Cars, Trucks & Crossovers increased significantly, taking into account the price crossovers were by far the largest contributor to the total dollar amount of leases.
Source: GM 10k SEC Filings
The problem here is that if we see a reversal in recent uptrend in crossovers, perhaps caused by higher gasoline prices, the rate of customers returning their crossover to GM dealers is likely to skyrocket. It is therefore no surprise that last year Mary Barra announced that within the next 18 months GM will add two more electric vehicles to its offering, both of which will be crossovers. A Great strategy to sign in its lease customers turning in their old ICE crossover for a new lease on an electric one.
The management has also taken important steps to curtail its inventory levels and kept on its promise in mid-2017 to reduce its inventory of unsold vehicles. Over the course of 2017, it reduced its inventory by more than $3bn or around 23%. As a result, inventory turnover has improved significantly, edging closer to that of Ford.
Source: Author's calculations based on GM SEC Filings
The net cash outflow from leasing operations has also improved significantly over the last year, despite the overall decrease in second hand car prices:
Source: GM 10k SEC Filings
Overall, I see the inventory and lease posing the biggest risk for GM right now, especially if these are triggered by a recession in the US and overall decline in total vehicle sales. Nevertheless, GM management has once again taken the right steps toward decreasing its inventory levels and improving efficiency, while at the same time ramping up its electric crossover offerings to retain the loyalty of its customers.
GM Valuation Although overall price, book and cash flow multiples suggest that GM is trading at a discount, valuing the overall company is much more complicated. After all, GM resembles more a bank that happens to sell cars. Add to that mix Cruise Automation and all Chinese JVs and you will get an idea why sum of the parts is the most appropriate approach here.
Source: GM
Therefore, my SOTP analysis values the following business units separately - GM Automotive (including the JVs), GM Financial & Cruise Automation.
WACC
My WACC calculation is based on the following assumptions:
Risk Free Rate - I assume 0.5% increase in current U.S. 10-year bond yields; the 3.5% rate is also consistent with Duff & Phelps normalized risk-free rate. Equity Risk Premium - again to be conservative I'm assuming 1.0% higher ERP than the one suggested by Aswath Damodaran. This higher ERP also factors the high exposure to the Chinese and other riskier markets. Beta - based on 5-year returns of GM and S&P 500. Cost of debt - based on GM weighted-average interest rate on outstanding long-term debt as quoted in GM's 2017 10k filing. Debt-to-Capital ratio - based on book value of short and long-term Automotive debt and current market cap. Tax Rate - assuming U.S. statutory corporate tax rate.
Source: Author's calculations, various data sources
GM Automotive & JVs - $73.5bn
To value GM Automotive, we first have to exclude current assets and Goodwill related to GM Financial. Ideally we have to separate out all PP&E related to GM Financial as well; however, as such information is not disclosed and the amount is likely to be immaterial I am using the whole amount of PP&E.
Source: Author's calculations based on GM SEC Filings
I then calculate Automotive EBIT using Automotive sales and the gross margin %. GM Financial interest is then excluded and Equity income from JVs is added.
Source: Author's calculations based on GM SEC Filings
To calculate business value of the automotive division, I am using a very conservative negative growth rate of 5% which aims to take into account expected decreases in vehicle sales in the U.S.
Source: Author's calculations based on GM SEC Filings
GM Financial - $4.0bn
I am valuing GM Financial at book value due to risks associated with operating leases exposure discussed above.
Source: Author's calculations based on GM SEC Filings
GM Cruise - $8.1bn
To arrive at the $8.1bn, I am assuming that the second tranche of SoftBank investment will be made 2 years from now, although GM expects AVs to be commercially available in 2019.
The discount rate is based on the one used by Aswath Damodaran in valuing Uber.
Source: Author's calculations
GM Intrinsic Value
Based on the values provided above, the sum of the parts valuation results in GM overall Enterprise Value of $85,616bn .
Source: Author's calculations based on GM SEC Filings
Even after making all very conservative assumptions listed above, my calculated target price for GM comes at $53.2 .
Conclusion GM is rapidly transforming itself from a classic ICE car manufacturer to a Silicon Valley tech giant. GM Cruise, acquired for only $581m two years ago, is now valued at $10bn. While getting ready for Auto 2.0, GM's core business is also performing very well with its Crossovers and Chevy Bolt being among the top selling in the U.S.
Risk regarding the vehicle sales cycle and the large lease exposure remain; however, the management is also busy addressing these by working on developing electric Crossovers which are likely to lure customers turning in their leased vehicles. How the whole cycle will play out is still hard to predict, in my opinion, and any downturn caused by a recession could be easily hedged through portfolio diversification.
Finally, GM's valuation still remains very conservative even after the nearly 20% increase in share price over the last month. Given the low price, long-term competitive advantages which would allow GM to retain its above average ROE to its OEM competitors and the strong management, I consider GM a great value stock in a lofty priced market.
Disclosure: I am/we are long GM.
